sheet-68.description: Sheet 68 shows the new residential district of Wyoming at 100 feet to an inch, turned so that north lies toward the upper right. Wyoming Avenue crosses the sheet from lower left to upper right as the main street, with Chestnut, Grand, Cedar and Cypress running at right angles to it between Prospect Avenue on the north and Myrtle Avenue on the south. Laurel Avenue bounds the district on the west, beside the curve of Glen Avenue, and the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad (Morris and Essex Division) swings across the lower left corner. The blocks are numbered 1 to 9 and are divided into narrow lots lettered along the street lines. Most lots are still empty; the houses stand scattered, many of them dwellings with outbuildings, and a few buildings are colored brick or stone. Near the junction of Wyoming Avenue and Grand Street are a fire station marked Wyoming Fire Co. No. 1 and a church, with a Presbyterian church near Wyoming Avenue and Cedar Street. North of Prospect Avenue the sheet shows large estate tracts, among them the property of John C. Willever with a house called The Knoll, running up to the edge of the South Mountain Reservation at the top of the sheet. Street widths of 60 and 75 feet are marked. Sheets 75, 70, 69, 1 and 3 are indexed on the margins.
notes: Grand Street is today Linden Street.
Glen Avenue was left out of the control: its modern line is about 10 m from the drawn one.
Walnut Avenue is lettered at the lower left edge, cut off by the sheet edge.
Wyoming district (Prospect, Wyoming, Myrtle avenues; Laurel, Chestnut, Grand, Cedar, Cypress), north to upper right. 100 ft. Glen Avenue left out (its junctions 10-11 m off the drawn line).

sheet-69.description: Sheet 69 lies south of Wyoming and shows the open land between the railroad and the East Branch of the Rahway River at 100 feet to an inch. At the top right are the lower ends of Chestnut, Grand, Cedar and Cypress streets meeting Myrtle Avenue, with a row of narrow lots, a greenhouse range and a few dwellings along its south side. The Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad (Morris and Essex Division) crosses the upper part of the sheet from the top centre toward the right edge. Ridgewood Road runs east and then curves across the sheet, and where it meets Millburn Avenue and Vaux Hall Road at the left edge the three roads form a wide fork. In the angle between Ridgewood Road and Millburn Avenue stands the Maplewood Poultry Farm, a house and a number of long coops. North of Ridgewood Road a plant for making hollow cement blocks stands on a large tract. East of the poultry farm a laid out tract (block 4) has Oakdale, Roland and Rosedale avenues running down toward Milton, all marked 50 feet wide, but with almost no buildings. The East Branch of the Rahway River crosses the lower left and marks the line between Essex County and Union County. A lot subdivision fills the top left corner, beside a house and shed at the sheet number.
notes: Grand Street is today Linden Street.
The drawn rotation (about 67 degrees) differs by about 5 degrees from sheet 68.
Myrtle Av to Milton, Ridgewood Rd, Millburn Av, Oakdale/Roland/Rosedale avenues, East Branch Rahway River. 100 ft.

sheet-70.description: Sheet 70 covers the western edge of Wyoming and the land along Millburn Avenue at 100 feet to an inch. Millburn Avenue crosses the sheet from lower left to right and Wyoming Avenue runs north from it to Laurel Avenue and Glen Avenue at the top. The Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad (Morris and Essex Division), several tracks wide, crosses the upper part of the sheet from lower left to upper right. Between the railroad and Millburn Avenue stand the Summit Water Works pumping station and a few dwellings and lots. East of Wyoming Avenue a large tract belonging to W. C. Whittingham holds a single house; Walnut Avenue and Myrtle Avenue run north from Millburn Avenue at the right edge, with a narrow row of lots and dwellings on Walnut Avenue. South of Millburn Avenue the sheet is mostly open land belonging to W. C. Wittingham and the Owen McCabe Estate. On the McCabe tract stand the buildings of the Carter-Bell Manufacturing Co., makers of artificial rubber products, marked as burned in July 1912. A few farm buildings and the bend of a stream occupy the lower right. Neighbouring sheets 68, 69 and 74 are indexed at the margins.
notes: Placed from Millburn Avenue junctions and a point carried from sheet 68; low confidence.
A street lettered Drive runs along the left edge; the full name could not be read.
Wyoming Av / Millburn Av, mostly open land. 100 ft. Three points (one detected, one hand-picked, one carried from sheet-68); low confidence.

sheet-71.description: Sheet 71 shows the south end of Millburn village along Main Street at 100 feet to an inch. Main Street runs down the right side of the sheet, curving to the southeast, with Spring Street meeting it at the top and Willow, Ocean and Mechanic streets branching west in turn. The lots on Main Street and Spring Street are narrow and mostly built with dwellings. West of Main Street, Willow Street ends at a block of empty land, and Ocean and Mechanic streets enclose a small block of lots with scattered houses; a large brick building stands on Mechanic Street. The line between Essex County and Union County crosses the lower part of the sheet; below it a cemetery occupies the land between Main Street and the river. The West Branch of the Rahway River winds down the left side of the sheet, with a Short Hills Water Co. pumping station beside it and the lines of buried water pipes crossing the open ground. The upper left is a large open tract with property lines only. A lane and further lots lead off Main Street at the lower right corner. Streets are marked 40, 45 and 50 feet wide.
notes: Orchard Street, between Ocean and Mechanic streets, is not named on the sheet.
South Millburn: Main St with Spring, Willow, Ocean, Mechanic; cemetery; Short Hills Water Co. pumping station. 100 ft.

sheet-72-1.description: The main map of sheet 72, at 100 feet to an inch, covers the thinly built land east of Main Street at the south-east end of Millburn village, from the mill pond near Rector Street south to the Essex County and Union County line. Main Street runs down the west edge of the sheet; the cross streets entering it from the west (Rector, Spring, Willow, Ocean and Mechanic streets) are drawn only as short stubs, since their blocks are on sheet 71. The east side of Main Street is lined with dwellings, sheds and hen houses on long narrow lots, and a Private Way runs east from Main Street opposite Mechanic Street. The West Branch of the Rahway River crosses the upper half of the sheet from north-west to east, widening into a pond above a dam, with a wooden bridge at the north edge. Beside the dam and race stand the Fandango Mills, makers of binder's board, with a fenced paper stock storage building; a note refers to the enlarged plan of the mill on the same sheet. The rest of the sheet is open land in large parcels, among them the property of Esther T. Woodruff with a dwelling and outbuildings near the south-east corner. A second pond lies at the east edge, and Springfield Avenue and the county line cross the south-east corner. The upper middle of the sheet is taken up by the inset with the enlarged plan of the Fandango Mills.
notes: The names of Rector, Willow, Ocean and Mechanic streets are cut off at the west edge of the sheet (printed in full on sheet 71).
The Private Way east of Main Street may correspond to part of modern Bleeker Street; not used for control.
Placed only from five junctions along Main Street (three detected, two hand-picked), so the east half of the sheet rests on the fitted rotation.

East of Main St south of the village: Fandango Mills on the West Branch Rahway River, county line. Two parts: 1 main map (100 ft; control only along Main St, helmert), 2 inset enlarged plan of Fandango Mills (50 ft, placed from corners carried from part 1).
placenames: West Branch of the Rahway River

sheet-72-2.description: The inset on sheet 72 is an enlarged plan, at 50 feet to an inch, of the Fandango Mills, manufacturers of binder's board, on the West Branch of the Rahway River east of Main Street in Millburn. It is drawn at the same orientation as the main map and enclosed in a heavy border at the top of the sheet. The plan shows the pond and dam, the head race and a small reservoir feeding the water wheel, and the long main mill building with rooms for grinding, rolling and making, mixing, drying and sorting, an engine and boiler room, dry rooms, a dusting and sorting room and an office, with the covered tail race leading back to the river. Separate buildings are a storage house near the river and a fenced paper stock storage building west of the mill, with a coal pile and a hydrant on the six-inch water pipe that comes in from Main Street. A long note records the fire protection: no watchman, the plant running day and night, steam heat and electric lights, coal fuel, Grinnell automatic sprinklers, a gravity tank and hose. The same mill appears at smaller scale on the main map of the sheet.
notes: Placed from seven building and fence corners carried from the main map of the sheet (sheet-72-1); its accuracy is that of the main map.

East of Main St south of the village: Fandango Mills on the West Branch Rahway River, county line. Two parts: 1 main map (100 ft; control only along Main St, helmert), 2 inset enlarged plan of Fandango Mills (50 ft, placed from corners carried from part 1).
placenames: West Branch of the Rahway River

sheet-73.description: Sheet 73 shows the centre of Millburn village at 100 feet to an inch, the area between the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad on the north and Spring Street on the south, with Main Street along the east edge and Blaine Street on the west. Millburn Avenue crosses the sheet from west to east as the main business street, with Essex and Elm streets north of it and Taylor, Church and Rector streets running east from Spring Street to Main Street south of it. The blocks along Main Street and Millburn Avenue are closely built with stores, dwellings and some brick buildings; the blocks to the south and west are residential, many of them divided into narrow lots that are still empty. Between the railroad and Elm Street stand the Millburn Electric Co. plant (engine and dynamo room, ice making and ice machine rooms, coal pockets and a trestle siding) and the car barn and shops of the Morris County Traction Co. Public School No. 2 stands on the south side of Millburn Avenue, with a fire department station and hook and ladder house near the Main Street corner. Churches shown are the Millburn Baptist Church on Millburn Avenue at Spring Street, the A.M.E. Zion Church on Church Street, and St. Stephen's Episcopal Church with St. Stephen's Parish Hall near Main Street. The former F. Fouratt hat factory on Church Street at Spring Street is marked vacant, and a range of greenhouses stands west of Essex Street. The north-west corner shows only street outlines marked not named and the railroad, which are drawn in full on sheet 76.
notes: Elm, the eastern continuation of Essex, is today part of Essex Street.
Two streets marked Not Named in the north-west corner, north of the railroad.
The north-south Spring between Millburn Avenue and Rector and the east-west Spring at the bottom of the sheet are both part of modern Spring Street.
Millburn village centre: Millburn Av, Essex/Elm, Taylor, Church, Rector, Spring, Blaine, Main; Millburn Electric Co. One part, 100 ft. Pilot sheet (ink 80: 14 points).

sheet-74.description: Sheet 74 shows the centre of Millburn village east of Main Street at 100 feet to an inch. Main Street runs down the left side of the sheet; Millburn Avenue crosses it near the top and curves east along the face of the village past Lackawanna Place and Depot Place. Taylor, Church, Rector and Spring streets and Elm Street meet Main Street from the west. North of Millburn Avenue stand the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad (Morris and Essex Division) passenger depot and freight station, with coal pockets and tracks, and the angle of Glen Avenue at the top. Millburn Avenue is built up with stores, a hotel and saloon, a garage and dwellings; the lots on Depot Place and Millburn Avenue are narrow and mostly occupied. A brook runs from the pond at the top left down Main Street, crossing the sheet to the lower left. South and east of Millburn Avenue the land is open, belonging to Mrs. Martha Whittingham, the C. A. Lighthipe estate and W. C. Whittingham, with a few farm buildings. A lumber yard and a coal pile with a trestle track stand near the brook. A wooden bridge carries Main Street over the brook near the bottom. The right edge is lettered Drive.
notes: Elm Street is today part of Essex Street.
Drive at the right edge is lettered without a visible name beyond that word.
Millburn village east of Main St: depot, Lackawanna Pl, Depot Pl, Millburn Av, Whittingham land. 100 ft.

sheet-75-1.description: The main map of sheet 75, at 100 feet to an inch, is drawn turned on the page with north to the right. It covers the mostly open land north-west of Millburn village between the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad on the left and the edge of the South Mountain Reservation on the right. Old Short Hills Road crosses the upper left corner and Brookside Drive runs along the top of the sheet from it towards the north. Glen Avenue climbs from the bottom of the sheet in a long curve to meet Brookside Drive near the upper right, and Lackawanna Place comes in from the left across the railroad to meet Glen Avenue. Along the railroad at the left are the passenger station and freight buildings of the Millburn depot with several sidings, and a spur track leads up across the middle of the sheet towards the Millburn Top Rock Co., a small group of buildings beside a stone quarry. The West Branch of the Rahway River winds across the upper part of the sheet below Brookside Drive, where the Diamond Mills Paper Co. stands on the drive; a note refers to the enlarged plan of the mill drawn in the inset at the lower right. The rest of the sheet is undeveloped land divided into a few large parcels, with the South Mountain Reservation lettered along the right edge and above the inset.
notes: Placed from three junctions only (Glen Avenue at Brookside Drive and at Lackawanna Place detected; Brookside Drive at Old Short Hills Road hand-picked between two modern nodes 33 m apart), so the fit has no redundancy.
Railroad crossings were not usable: the modern line is not crossed at grade by Lackawanna Place.

North-west of the village, turned with north to the right: Glen Av, Brookside Drive, Old Short Hills Rd, Lackawanna Pl, depot, Millburn Top Rock Co. Two parts: 1 main map (100 ft, three junctions), 2 inset enlarged plan of Diamond Mills Paper Co. (50 ft, carried from part 1).

sheet-75-2.description: The inset at the lower right of sheet 75 is an enlarged plan, at 50 feet to an inch, of the Diamond Mills Paper Co. on Brookside Drive, on the West Branch of the Rahway River north-west of Millburn village. It is drawn at the same orientation as the main map, with north to the right, inside a heavy border below the lettering of the South Mountain Reservation. The plan shows the long machine room with a 45 horsepower engine, the bleaching and chopping building at road level, a mixing room, the beating, rag and paper storage building, the engine and boiler house with a 350 horsepower engine, a bridge and a bulkhead at the water's edge, and a separate storage and machine shop with a shed that is marked not sprinklered. Hydrants with hose, underground tanks and water tanks are marked around the buildings, and a note at the right records the night watchman, heating, power, the Grinnell and Walworth sprinkler systems and the fire pails. The same mill is drawn at smaller scale at the top of the main map.
notes: Placed from seven building corners carried from the main map of the sheet (sheet-75-1); its accuracy is that of the main map.

North-west of the village, turned with north to the right: Glen Av, Brookside Drive, Old Short Hills Rd, Lackawanna Pl, depot, Millburn Top Rock Co. Two parts: 1 main map (100 ft, three junctions), 2 inset enlarged plan of Diamond Mills Paper Co. (50 ft, carried from part 1).

sheet-76.description: Sheet 76 shows the Old Short Hills Road district west of Millburn village at 100 feet to an inch, with north toward the left of the sheet. Old Short Hills Road crosses the sheet from lower left to upper right as the main road, meeting Marion Avenue and Hobart Avenue at a three-way junction near the centre, with Brookside Drive running along the top to a second junction at the upper right. Hillside Avenue runs down the left side of the sheet, and Hobart Avenue runs south from the central junction to the bottom. East of Hobart Avenue the Brison tract is laid out in blocks 5 to 9 with streets marked Not Named, divided into many narrow empty lots and bounded on the right by the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad. The few buildings stand on large estate lots north and west of the roads: the properties of F. C. Farley, W. W. McCullum, Williams, Denman, George Campbell, the Brook Lawn Co., A. J. Parkhurst and Anna G. Campbell, with dwellings, outbuildings and a greenhouse. A building marked as fire ruins stands near the right side. The lower left corner shows a large brick building on its own lot. Street widths of 30 to 62 feet are marked.
notes: Placed from Old Short Hills Road junctions only; low confidence (helmert).
Several streets of the Brison tract are lettered Not Named.
Old Short Hills Rd / Brookside Drive / Marion / Hobart / Hillside avenues, David Brison tract; north to the left. 100 ft. Two-point helmert; low confidence.

sheet-77.description: Sheet 77 shows a largely open estate district of Old Short Hills at 100 feet to an inch, drawn turned so that north lies toward the upper left. Jefferson Avenue runs down the left edge past a row of dwellings on large lots, including those of Wm. Hill, Jenkinson and David M. Lewis, and continues as Montview Avenue, which curves south-east across the sheet to Highland Avenue along the bottom. Hillside Avenue enters at the top right and becomes Hobart Avenue, which runs down the right side to Highland Avenue. Belwick Lane crosses the middle of the sheet between Montview Avenue and Hillside Avenue. Most of the sheet is undeveloped land divided by faint property lines into large tracts. The L. G. Kaufman estate has a large reinforced concrete building drawn in blue, with smaller outbuildings, and the Mrs. Mary Nadin and A. H. Marckwald places have single dwellings. Near Hobart Avenue stand the greenhouse ranges of John Wilson, florist, and E. C. McFadden, florist, and at the bottom the Stewart Hartshorn place with outbuildings and the lots of E. P. Carrington and E. Axtell. Water pipes run along Montview, Hobart and Highland avenues. The sheet joins sheets 78, 79, 80, 82, 76 and 87.
notes: Belwick Lane is Delwick Lane in OpenStreetMap; the modern line differs from the drawn one near Montview Avenue.

Names checked by the lead on the overview: William Hill is an owner label (Wm. Hill homestead), not a street; Knollwood Pl. added at the bottom edge. Monroe Terrace is not in the OpenStreetMap extract.
Old Short Hills estates: Jefferson, Montview, Hillside, Hobart, Belwick Lane, Highland; north to the left. 100 ft. Four hand-picked points (RMSE 5 m); low confidence.

sheet-78.description: Sheet 78 shows the north-western part of Old Short Hills at 100 feet to an inch, turned so that north lies toward the upper left. The sheet is mostly open ground: the upper third is taken by the South Mountain Reservation, the West Branch Rahway River and a pond, with Brookside Drive running south-east beside the water to the Marion Avenue corner at the right edge. Old Short Hills Road crosses the lower half from the left edge to the right, meeting Farley Road, Glen Avenue and Washington Avenue at a wide junction near the left, and Hillside Avenue near the right edge. Farley Road runs up the left side past the Short Hills Farm, whose farm buildings, a cow barn and a pond stand inside the loop it makes with Glen Avenue; the dwelling named Burnside and a smaller house for Sarah K. Cox stand within the same ground. South of Old Short Hills Road lie the estates of Albert D. Traphagen, A. H. Block, Alice L. Simpson and the Brooklawn Co., each shown as a large lot with one or two dwellings and outbuildings. At the lower left the Marshall Geer property is bounded by Jefferson and Washington avenues and includes a large pink-coloured building labelled as a tile company works. Street widths of 50 to 62 feet are lettered on the roads. Adjoining sheets 75, 76, 77 and 79 are numbered at the edges.
notes: Brookside Avenue-era Brookside Drive, Old Short Hills Road, Glen Avenue, Marion Avenue and Hillside Avenue keep their names today.
A street at the lower left edge is cut off and its name is only partly legible (ending in -dison Terrace).
The wide junction of Old Short Hills Road, Farley Road, Glen Avenue and Washington Avenue is a single modern node (Glen Avenue / Old Short Hills Road, with Washington Avenue about 11 m away).
The loop of Farley Road into Glen Avenue is not at the modern Farley Road / Glen Avenue node, which lies close to the main junction; that modern node was not used.
Old Short Hills north-west: Old Short Hills Rd, Glen Av, Farley Rd, Brookside Drive; north to upper left. 100 ft. Four points; low confidence.

sheet-79.description: Sheet 79 shows part of Old Short Hills west of sheet 78 at 100 feet to an inch, turned so that north lies toward the upper left. Old Short Hills Road runs from the top left down the left side and then south-east across the sheet to the right edge, with Farley Road leaving it near the top and curving east toward a pond at the upper right. The land is held as large estates: E. Todd with a dwelling named Sun Dial Court at the top, Richard Hopkins with Beauvoir, Henry E. Bailey, J. M. Gallagher, S. B. Denman, Laura M. Issacs with Cristal Springs, and E. B. Renwick with Brook Lawn along the east side of Old Short Hills Road. West of the road stand John Taylor's Woodfield, E. B. Sutphen's Stonyside and T. Y. Sutphen's White Gables. South of the road White Oak Ridge Road runs south-west from its junction with Old Short Hills Road, crossing Parsonage Hill Road, which continues west to the left edge, and ends near Adams Avenue. Jefferson Avenue runs south-west from Old Short Hills Road along the east side of the lots of A. F. Riach, Stephen Nash and A. S. Learoyd, meeting Washington Avenue, Madison Terrace and, near the foot, Monroe Terrace and Adams Avenue. The blocks between these streets are laid out as lots but have almost no buildings. The compass at the left edge gives the turned orientation, and the adjoining sheets 77, 78 and 80 are numbered at the margins.
notes: White Oak Ridge Road appears to be the part of modern Parsonage Hill Road south-east of the Old Short Hills Road junction (identity from the position of the modern road, not a printed name).
Madison Terrace and Jefferson Avenue are kept under those names in the modern street network; Monroe Terrace is not found under that name.
Reading made from the 1600 px overview at the printed lettering size; small lot-owner names were not transcribed.
Old Short Hills: Old Short Hills Rd, Farley Rd, White Oak Ridge Rd, Jefferson, Washington, Madison Ter. 100 ft. LOO 12 m; low confidence.

sheet-80.description: Sheet 80 shows a district of Old Short Hills at 100 feet to an inch, drawn with north toward the top. Forest Drive runs down the left side from the top corner to Highland Avenue at the lower left, and Western Drive runs east from it, curves south and continues down the middle of the sheet, crossing East Lane and Jefferson Avenue and meeting Montview Avenue near the foot. Montview Avenue runs north-east to the Jefferson Avenue junction; Belwick Lane leaves it toward the lower right. Adams Avenue and Jefferson Avenue enclose a block of small lots at the upper right between Adams Avenue and Monroe Terrace, with Madison Terrace and White Oak Ridge Road at the top right edge. Two unnamed roads at the upper left are lettered No Name. The ground is almost all estate land with large houses and grounds: G. Haswell, Page Chapman, Wm M. Deen, Stewart Hartshorn, C. M. Johnson and Mrs. B. Bryne, whose house is named Montview; a house for each of Wm Hill No. 3 and No. 6 stands on the Monroe Terrace block. A reservoir stands beside Western Drive south of Jefferson Avenue. A lake lies at the top left corner. Eight-inch and six-inch water pipes are marked in most of the roads. The right-hand lower area is blank and belongs to sheet 77; sheets 79, 87 and 88 adjoin at the edges.
notes: Belwick Lane is modern Delwick Lane.
The north-south part of Western Drive is modern Lake Road; the east-west part keeps the name Western Drive.
Monroe Terrace is modern Birch Lane (position match, not a printed name).
Two streets at the upper left are lettered No Name.
Old Short Hills: Forest Drive, Western Drive, East Lane, Montview, Highland, lake. North up, 100 ft.

sheet-81.description: Sheet 81 covers the thinly built land along Millburn Avenue between Millburn village and Short Hills Road, south of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad (Morris and Essex Division), which crosses the top of the sheet. Millburn Avenue runs across the middle of the sheet from Short Hills Road at the left to the edge of sheet 73 at the right, and Short Hills Road runs up the left side to Pine Terrace East. On Short Hills Road north of Millburn Avenue stand St. Rose's Roman Catholic Church and St. Rose's Parochial School, with St. Rose's Cemetery behind them, and further north a disused building of the Short Hills Water Co. St. Stephen's Episcopal Cemetery lies north of Millburn Avenue in the middle of the sheet. The rest of the land is in large holdings, among them those of Stewart Hartshorn, Elizabeth Bodwell, Dr. W. M. Barnes, the W. Campbell estate and Hannah J. Smith, with a few dwellings and outbuildings. Water pipes cross the sheet diagonally. At the lower left the East Branch of the Rahway River marks the boundary between Essex and Union counties, and at the right edge a short street runs south from Millburn Avenue towards Rector Street; two streets marked not named appear at the top right beyond the railroad.
notes: The printed scale bar (Scale of Feet, 0 to 150) corresponds to 50 ft to an inch, but the sheet is drawn at 100 ft to an inch: the fitted 4.07 px/ft and the spacing of the Short Hills Road junctions (959 ft drawn, 988 ft today) agree with 100 ft.
Short Hills Rd. is today Short Hills Avenue.
The north arrow points about 15 degrees off the fitted north; the fitted rotation is supported by the directions of both Short Hills Road and Millburn Avenue.
Placed by a two-point helmert from junctions along Short Hills Road; low confidence.

Millburn Av between the village and Short Hills Rd, St. Rose church and cemetery. Drawn at 100 ft although the scale bar (Scale of Feet 0-150) reads as 50 ft; two-point helmert on Short Hills Rd; low confidence.

sheet-82.description: Sheet 82 covers the heart of the Short Hills estate district at 100 feet to an inch, with its streets curving through large private grounds. In the north-west corner Hillside Avenue and Hobart Avenue meet at a bend beside the Millburn High School, a pink-coloured brick building with its heating, lighting and chemistry notes, standing among small residential lots lettered with the owners Mrs. Coen, A. Wittkop, H. Wittkop, Mrs. Baldwin and A. McFadden. Hobart Avenue then runs south-west past the open grounds of Stewart Hartshorn, whose large property takes up most of the middle of the sheet and is lettered The Crescent. Within it stand a mansion, a green house and several outbuildings and dwellings, among them Arowyn, the house of E. P. S. Wright, with its auto houses. The Crescent and Crescent Place curve around a group of estate lots (L. W. Harrington, C. Goodrich and more Hartshorn land), where a fire alarm box is marked on Crescent Place. A railroad of several tracks crosses the sheet diagonally from the bottom left towards the top right. Near the bottom Baltusrol Way crosses it, and two long buildings stand by the tracks. Short Hills Road runs across the lower right with a row of small lots and dwellings on its north side, joined by Overlook Terrace and Pine Terrace East. Water pipes of 3 to 8 inches are drawn along the streets and across the open ground. Much of the right half of the sheet is blank, being unbuilt ground. A heavy-lined street across the top is marked Not Named. The adjoining sheets are numbered 76, 77, 81, 84 and 87 on the margins.
notes: Belwick Lane is today Delwick Lane.
Short Hills Road is today part of Short Hills Avenue.
A street across the top of the sheet is lettered Not Named.
The Crescent is the name of the Stewart Hartshorn estate (in quotation marks on the sheet) as well as of the curved street.
Short Hills: Hobart Av, Highland Av, The Crescent, Short Hills Rd, Baltusrol Way; north to upper left. 100 ft. LOO 9 m; low confidence.

sheet-83.description: Sheet 83 covers the south-eastern part of Short Hills at 100 feet to an inch, turned so that north lies towards the left of the page. Short Hills Road crosses the top of the sheet, with Millburn Avenue running south from it along the Essex County and Union County line to Morris Turnpike at the bottom right. In the west the sheet shows a grid of laid-out but largely unbuilt streets: Pine Terrace East, Campbell Road, Wellington Avenue East and West, Meadow Brook Avenue, Baltusrol Way, Elmwood Place and Woodland Road, several of them marked not graded and all given widths of 50 to 60 feet. The blocks between them are numbered 1 to 8 and are empty. East of Millburn Avenue, a branch of the Rahway River flows south-west to north-east across the upper right, and a water pipe crosses the top right corner. Buildings appear only along the east side of Millburn Avenue and towards Morris Turnpike: the greenhouses of J. F. Anderson, florist, several dwellings and outbuildings, and a group at the junction with Summit Road and Morris Turnpike, where the Klaus Stemmermann estate and the name C. Pierson are lettered. The lower left, below Woodland Road, holds only property lines and is drawn on sheets 84 and 85. A compass rose and the 100 foot scale bar are printed on the sheet.
notes: Wellington Avenue East and West, Meadow Brook Avenue and Elmwood Place are marked not graded.
The street at the right edge ending in 'Drive' and the road at the bottom right ending in 'Road' are cut off at the sheet edge.
Modern Baltusrol Way follows the street drawn here as Baltusrol Way; Campbell Road, Wellington Avenue and Woodland Road survive under the same names.
Short Hills south-east: Campbell Rd, Wellington Av, Meadow Brook Av, Baltusrol Way, Millburn Av, Morris Turnpike. 100 ft.

sheet-84.description: Sheet 84 shows the centre of Short Hills at 100 feet to an inch, north to the top. The Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad, Morris and Essex Division, crosses the upper part from west to east, with the Short Hills Station and two passenger depots on its south side. Hobart Avenue and Knollwood Road meet the line at the top left, and Chatham Road runs along its south side to Short Hills Road, which leaves at the right and runs south-east. Baltusrol Way is the long street running down the right-centre of the sheet, crossed by Overlook Terrace, Ridge Terrace, Fernwood Terrace, Pine Terrace East and West and Wellington Avenue West and East; Woodland Road forms the west side of the grid. The blocks are numbered 1 to 7 and carry detached frame dwellings, mostly on large lots, a pink-marked building near Ridge Terrace and one by Short Hills Road, and the greenhouses of Thomas Jones, florist, at the left, with a Fire Department hose house (Hose No. 3) at the far left. A water pipe follows the railroad and Short Hills Road. Several of the street widths (35 to 50 feet) are lettered along the kerbs. Sheet numbers 82, 83 and 86 mark the adjoining sheets.
notes: Fernwood Terrace is not in the OpenStreetMap extract under that name; Fernwood Road exists elsewhere in Short Hills.

Baltusrol Way, Woodland Road, Pine Terrace East and West, Ridge Terrace, Overlook Terrace, Campbell Road and Wellington Avenue keep their names today. Ridge Terrace and Woodland Road form a curved corner that was left out of the control points.
Short Hills centre: railroad and station, Chatham Rd, Hobart Av, Pine Terraces, Woodland Rd. 100 ft.

sheet-86.description: Sheet 86, at 100 feet to an inch, is drawn turned on the page with north towards the upper right. It covers open land in the south of Short Hills, west of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad (Morris and Essex Division), which runs down the right side of the sheet in a cutting crossed by two bridges. Chatham Road runs beside the railroad on its west side and Hobart Avenue on its east side; from Hobart Avenue the short ends of Taylor Road, Northern Drive, Forest Drive and Knollwood Road lead off the right edge into the residential sheets 87 and 90. Nearly all the rest of the sheet is large undivided parcels belonging to Stewart Hartshorn, the developer of Short Hills, with one parcel of John Kane; the only buildings are a carpenter shop and a shed beside Chatham Road and part of a building at the bottom edge by the railroad. At the bottom left Woodland Road curves into Ridge Terrace, with Fernwood Terrace leading off it, at the edge of the built-up district of sheet 84.
notes: Control lies mostly along Hobart Avenue (four junctions); the fifth point, Woodland Road at Ridge Terrace, is hand-picked at a curve, so the west half of the sheet is weakly controlled.
Fernwood Terrace is not in the modern street data under that name (a Fernwood Road exists).

Short Hills south, turned with north to the upper right: Chatham Road and Hobart Av along the railroad, Stewart Hartshorn land; Woodland Rd / Ridge Ter at bottom. One part, 100 ft; control mostly along Hobart Av.

sheet-87.description: Sheet 87 shows the Stewart Hartshorn estate district of Short Hills at 100 feet to an inch, a hillside of large private grounds cut by curving drives. Chatham Road and the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western railroad run down the west edge, with Hobart Avenue beside the tracks. A steel bridge crosses the railroad near the top and again at the Forest Drive crossing. Northern Drive forms the north boundary of the built ground. Park Place runs south from it to Knollwood Road, and Forest Drive crosses the sheet from Park Place to Highland Avenue, joined on the way by Chestnut Place and Knollwood Road. Most of the lots are the property of Stewart Hartshorn, with other dwellings lettered for Mrs. H. Harriet, F. C. Harriman, F. G. Winston, G. Rand, M. R. Robertson, John Poncet, J. R. Strong, Mrs. Geo. C. Cobby, Mrs. Geo. Richmond, R. W. Little (with a house called Redstone), H. E. Welles (Chalet), James Brown (The Knoll), Maurice Sylvester (Crown Dale), Mrs. Wills and Mrs. E. D. Bliss (Greystones). The houses are frame dwellings with outbuildings and auto houses, and a few are marked brick or stone. At the bottom left Hobart Avenue runs past the Short Hills Casino, with tennis courts below it and two small buildings beside the railroad. Water pipes of 3 to 8 inches follow the drives. Wide areas of the sheet, especially the large numbered blocks 1, 2 and 5, are unbuilt ground. Highland Avenue and Montview Avenue appear at the lower right, and the neighbouring sheets are numbered 77, 80, 82, 84, 86, 88 and 90 on the margins.
notes: Knollwood Place, running north from Hobart Avenue to Knollwood Road, appears to be today's Wells Lane (position match only; modern name not confirmed from the sheet).
Highland Avenue and Montview Avenue were left out of the georeferencing: their modern lines sat 5 to 6 m off the drawn ones.
Chatham Road and Hobart Avenue beside the railroad are cut off by the sheet edge to the south; Hobart Avenue continues on sheet 82.
Short Hills estates: Park Place, Forest Drive, Knollwood Rd, Northern Drive, railroad at the west edge. 100 ft. Highland Av, Wells Lane, Montview left out (5-6 m off); south-east uncontrolled.

sheet-88.description: Sheet 88 shows the northern part of the Short Hills estate district at 100 feet to an inch, a hillside of large grounds laid out around winding drives. Forest Drive runs along the top of the sheet and again at the west and east edges, and a pond is drawn in the north-west corner. Highland Avenue curves across the upper middle from the west edge to the east, crossed by Western Drive, which runs south from Forest Drive and divides into Taylor Road, and by East Lane. Near East Lane stands the Short Hills Academy, a private school owned by Stewart Hartshorn and heated by hot water and lighted by electricity, and at the east edge Christ Episcopal Church with a heating furnace and electric lighting. Taylor Road crosses the lower part of the sheet from Minnisink Ridge, and Moraine Road curves along the south-west corner. Knollwood Road runs from Chestnut Place and the sheet 87 side up to the east edge, and Northern Drive branches off it near the bottom. Most lots are Stewart Hartshorn land, with dwellings lettered for H. S. Leavitt, T. W. Lloyd, Andrew Brown, B. C. Fincke, O. A. Schrieber, John Farr, D. P. Kingsford, M. L. Foster, Ashton Harvey (Cedarcrest), W. Fellows Morgan (Oak Knoll), Samuel Daviloge, A. K. Gardiner (Bearyfield), J. J. Carty, Mrs. H. P. Towler and L. L. Sturges. A private way runs through the Morgan and Harvey grounds. Water pipes of 4 and 8 inches follow the drives. The large blank areas at the right and bottom belong to the neighbouring sheets, numbered 80, 87 and 90 on the margins.
notes: Minnisink Ridge Road is read from a label split into Minnisink Ridge and Road along the west edge; medium confidence on the full name.
Taylor Road of this sheet (the part running south from Western Drive) is today partly Stewart Road and Taylor Place (position match only).
Moraine Road is today Moraine Place (position match only).
Chestnut Place / Knollwood Road was not detected and is not among the control points.
Short Hills: Highland Av, Western Drive, East Lane, Knollwood Rd, Taylor Rd; north to upper left. 100 ft.

sheet-89.description: Sheet 89, at 100 feet to an inch, is drawn turned on the page with north towards the upper left. It covers open land in the south of Short Hills between the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad (Morris and Essex Division), which sweeps across the sheet in a long curve, and the Morris Turnpike along the bottom, which is also the boundary between Essex and Union counties. At the top Hobart Avenue runs to Taylor Road and the railroad bridge, beyond which Chatham Road continues. South Terrace runs down the left side of the sheet from Hobart Avenue, with the ends of East Road and Coniston Road leading off it to the west into sheets 90 and 92. Almost all the land east of the railroad, and the triangle west of it, belongs to Stewart Hartshorn and is unbuilt. The only buildings are a few dwellings, a storage building and outbuildings along the north side of the Morris Turnpike near the railroad, which passes over the turnpike on a stone culvert, and some dwellings south of the turnpike at the lower left. A road leaves the turnpike southward at the lower right edge.
notes: Placed from three junctions in the upper left only (Hobart Avenue at Taylor Road and at South Terrace detected, Coniston Road at South Terrace hand-picked); the Morris Turnpike end of the sheet is extrapolated.
East Road is not in the modern street data.
The street names were read from the overview and a full-resolution crop of the upper left; the lettering is large.
Railroad curve and Morris Turnpike, Hartshorn land; Hobart Av, South Ter, Coniston Rd at the top. 100 ft. Three points in the upper left; low confidence.

sheet-90.description: Sheet 90 covers the south-western edge of Short Hills at 100 feet to an inch, turned so that north lies towards the left of the page. The Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad, Morris and Essex Division, curves down the right side, with Chatham Road beside it at the top right. Taylor Road crosses the upper part, with Northern Drive and Park Place above it and Knollwood Road at the left. Hobart Avenue runs diagonally from Taylor Road at the right towards the bottom centre, where it meets Coniston Road; South Terrace, East Road, Windemere Terrace and Hemlock Road lead off to the south and east. Blocks 1 to 7 are mostly large estates: Stewart Hartshorn's holdings at the top, the properties of Tysilio Thomas and Gilbert C. Brown (Twin Oaks) in the middle, and smaller lots with dwellings along South Terrace and Coniston Road, among them the Security and Realty Co., Craig and Roach Realty Co., C. W. L. Roche and B. V. H. Schultz. Several buildings are pink or blue for different constructions. The streets are 35 to 50 feet wide, with widths lettered at the kerbs. The left half of the sheet is open land divided only by property lines. The adjoining sheets 86, 87, 88, 89 and 92 are numbered at the margins.
notes: Modern Hobart Avenue, Taylor Road, South Terrace, Coniston Road and Windemere Terrace match these streets within a few metres.
The sheet carries a 100 foot scale bar at the lower left.
Hobart Av / Taylor Rd / South Ter / Coniston Rd / Windemere Ter; north to the left. 100 ft.
